subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S PERFORMANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to the latest economic indicators, the economy in Quebec continues to show sustained growth in 1985.
Thanks to our policies, 89,000 new jobs were created since September 1984. The unemployment rate, which was 12.8 per cent in September 1984, dropped to 11.8 per cent in October 1985, a net reduction of 1 per cent.
Between January and August 1985, amounts for which building permits were issued increased 23.3 per cent, as compared with the same period under the former Government.
The private sector is responding favourably to the First initiatives taken by our Government.
According to a recent survey conducted by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, 37 per cent of small- and medium-sized businesses intend to increase capital spending by the end of this year. Furthermore, 26 per cent are planning to hire staff, and 41 per cent expect to increase their working capital.

November 20, 1985
The estimated value of deliveries by the manufacturing sector as a whole has increased by $611 million over one year, an increase of 12.7 per cent.
Retail sales increased by 8 per cent during the same period.

As far as the economy is concerned, and especially that of Quebec and the riding of Chambly which I represent, the Mulroney team has managed to restore the confidence of investors and of Canadian entrepreneurship.

When stylish Raisa Gorbachev arrived in Geneva she wore an eye-catching tailored grey coat with a fur collar and matching fur hat. Several hours later Nancy Reagan appeared in an elegant mink coat and matching hat.

subsubtopic: HIGH INTEREST RATES CHARGED BY CREDIT CARD COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak on behalf of the 16 million Canadians who hold credit cards, particularly those who are paying outrageous interest rates on their unpaid balances month after month.
Credit card interest rates are essentially unchanged since 1983 and, in many cases, unchanged since the high interest rate period of 1981. The range is from 28.8 per cent for department store cards, to 24 per cent for oil company cards, down to 21 per cent and to 17.4 per cent for bank credit cards such as Visa and MasterCard.
Many low-income consumers who shop with these cards are getting no benefit from the general fall in interest rates. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has repeatedly told the House that he will not intercede on behalf of these consumers, many of whom do not qualify for lower interest loan credit. Instead, while he expresses his great faith in the market-place, the banks offer lower credit card rates to retailers but not to their consumers. Now the banks are offering gold cards, at a cost of up to $75 per year, with lower interest rates, to their upper-income customers who seldom need them because they pay their accounts promptly.
When the Conservative Government boasts of lower interest rates, we ask: lower interest rates for whom? There are lower interest rates for organized retailers and lower interest rates on credit cards for the well-off who do not need them. However, there are the same high rates for millions of average and low-income Canadians who cannot afford them.
I call upon the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) to take up the problems and the difficulties of low-income people who are being ripped off.
November 20, 1985

subsubtopic: FOOTWEAR IMPORT QUOTAS-STATEMENT OF MINISTER FOR INTERNATIONAL TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a year ago the Government announced an agenda for the economic renewal of Canada. In it, we recognize that Canada's economic well-being will be determined, in large part, by how successfully Canadians respond to the challenges of technological change and rising competition that are facts of life in today's world.
In the Agenda for Economic Renewal, we set ourselves four basic goals: to put our fiscal house in order; to make Government less intrusive, reducing the compulsive regulation that has hamstrung business and sapped it of creative energy; to adopt policies that foster higher investment, greater innovation and increased international competitiveness, and to do all this in a climate of fairness and openness that is characteristic of Canadian society.
One of the basic tenets of the agenda was that we must improve our export performance. Trade is our lifeblood. Nearly one-third of our national income and more than three million jobs are directly dependent on our exports. During the past year, promoting and improving our capacity to export has been one of our Government's main preoccupations. Securing our access to the bigest market, the United States, has of course been a major theme. But we have also launched an important trade initiative in the Pacific Rim. We have worked with the provincial Governments to draw up a dynamic national trade strategy, and we have taken a leading role in promoting and preparing for a new round of multilateral trade negotiations that would lower more of the barriers to commerce throughout the world.
Trade is a two-way street. To export, we must also import. The balance in our trade can only be determined by our capacity to compete. Artificial barriers, such as quotas and high tariff walls, may provide temporary protection to specific industries, but experience has taught us that they are counterproductive in the long run. They can have the effect of isolating the industries they were intended to protect, of making them less able, rather than more able, to stand on their own.
During the past year, Mr. Speaker, the Government has been engaged in a comprehensive policy review related to one of Canada's protected industries, footwear. Our producers of
November 20, 1985

footwear have enjoyed the protection of import quotas for the past eight years.
In June of last year, the previous Government assigned the Canadian Import Tribunal to review the industry's position, with particular stress on determining two factors: the extent of injury the footwear sector would sustain if quotas were lifted, and the extent to which the industry had used the period of protection to become more competitive.
To carry out its mandate, the Canadian Import Tribunal spent one year conducting the most comprehensive review ever undertaken of our footwear industry. In addition to its own studies, the tribunal heard 72 witnesses and received 39 written submissions representing virtually all interests, manufacturers, importers, exporters, retailers, labour unions and consumers. It made its report this past June, and we see no reason to disagree with its findings.
Indeed, the tribunal found great cause for optimism. It found that, by and large, the Canadian footwear industry has in recent years matched and, at times, outperformed the economy as a whole and the manufacturing sector in particular.
We now have an industry which has undergone a process of adaption, adjustment and change. It has made significant changes in product mix. It has strengthened its position in its most favourable market segments. It has thought up new methods of competing. It has improved the efficiency of its management and financial information systems. It has continued to employ state-of-the-art technology and has moved upward in the quality scale in the market.
As a result, we now have an industry that, with one temporary and limited exception-that of the makers of women's and girls' footwear-is ready to stand up to the international challenge.
The tribunal pointed out another relevant detail about the transformation of the footwear industry. The quota system had little effect on it. The changes were brought about primarily by the pressures of the market-place rather than eight years of quota protection. A particular source of the industry strength, for example, has been its ability to fill orders for short runs of new products on very short notice.
The Government has therefore concluded that further granting of import relief to the whole industry would not be in the country's economic interest. Accordingly, effective December 1, 1985, import controls will be continued only on women's and girls' dress and casual footwear. This sector accounts for nearly half of the Canadian industry sales, and it is the only sector which the Canadian Import Tribunal found would be injured by an immediate removal of quotas. Moreover, in this sector of the industry the tribunal recommended-and the Government is committed to it-a phasing out of quotas over the next three years. They will be increased by 6 per cent in the first year, 8 per cent in the second and 10 per cent in the third year. By then the quotas will have been in force for almost 11 years.
Statements by Ministers
In coming to this decision, the Government was influenced by the actual effects which the footwear quotas have had. They have driven shoe prices up. Canadian consumers have paid somewhere between $450 million and $500 million more for footwear than they would have, had there been no quotas. This increase has been felt by most lower-income Canadians, both because their budgets are lower and because low-cost imports have been restricted. Because prices were higher, demand for footwear decreased. Judging by the figures produced by the import tribunal, Canadian consumers now buy roughly 12 per cent fewer shoes than they would have if quotas had not been in force since 1978.
At the same time, the benefits accorded to the industry were minimal. In 1983, for example, consumers paid an extra $85 million for their footwear, while the industry produced only $29 million more than it would have without the protection of quotas.
Who gained from the quota system? The principal beneficiaries were not Canadian footwear producers. The ones who gained the most were the holders of footwear quotas, mostly importers and large retail chains. Smaller outlets were adversely affected because they had allocations too small to take advantage of price reductions for bulk buying.
There is a broader consideration as well in the Government decision to reduce and phase out footwear quotas. The fact is that continuation of the quotas would have seriously affected Canadian interests in other sectors of the economy.
The imposition of quotas invariably raises demands for compensation by countries whose exports are affected. These demands are neither unfair nor unrealistic. They are provided for by the rules of the international trading system which Canada supports. However, they are very expensive.
Compensation can take many forms-lower duties on other imports, for example, cash compensation or higher duties for some of our own exports. Injured countries are even entitled to retaliate by imposing their own quotas on products we sell to them.
Some Members of the House will recall that at the time the present footwear quotas were extended to November, 1985, the European Economic Community threatened to exercise its right to retaliate. It threatened to raise tariffs to prohibitive levels on Canadian petrochemicals, steel products, craft paper, furs and other products. This could have cost us $150 million in sales to Europe in industries that had nothing to do with footwear. We managed to stave off this threat only by agreeing to forgo duties on a range of European imports at a cost of $12 million to the Canadian Treasury. Had we not done so, a great many jobs would have been lost. This, somehow, does not seem fair.
The Government does not subscribe to the gloom and doom predictions that the lifting of quotas would result in the eventual demise of the Canadian footwear industry. The evidence suggests just the opposite, that the footwear industry has regained its vitality and health. It should not be forgotten,
Statements by Ministers
moreover, that Canadian manufacturers will still be protected by a 23 per cent tariff on imported footwear. Twenty-three per cent is a lot of protection. In the U.S., the average footwear tariff is 8 per cent; in western Europe, it is 10 per cent; and Canada's average tariff on all manufactured goods is 9 per cent.
The process of industry adjustment has been significant. It has, moreover, been speeded by a number of Government assistance programs. We estimate that by the time disbursements are finalized under the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board program, footwear companies accounting for more than 60 per cent of industry sales will have received benefits, benefits totalling $22.5 million. This assistance has been directed to management, finance, marketing and production, with the bulk of planned investments directed to upgrading equipment.
Additionally, I am pleased to announce that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will give consideration to any industry requests for temporary tariff or duty remission schemes to help the Canadian footwear industry improve its competitive position. These measures, coupled with Canada's existing antidumping legislation and the industry's increased competitiveness, not to mention the 23 per cent tariff, should allow Canadian manufacturers to compete successfully against foreign imports.
The Government anticipates that the lifting of quotas will give rise to a moderate surge in imports. Some of this will be due to pent-up demand for lower priced shoes. Some of it will be due to the fact that there will be a number of new importers, and some will be caused by what we expect will be an inclination by retailers to experiment by importing new items.
Our view is that the surge will be short-lived, that it will stabilize within 12 months to 18 months. Nevertheless, to mitigate any effects the surge may have, we will be conducting consultations with the countries which are Canada's principal footwear suppliers. We will put them on notice that their long-term interests in the Canadian market would best be served by a prudent and gradual approach to sales.
As for Canadian importers, some of whom have been known to bring in footwear for the sole purpose of establishing a high base for the allocation of future quotas, I will make it abundantly clear to them that such practices will not be rewarded in the future.
Canadians across the country will benefit as consumers from this decision. However, the Government also recognizes that a period of adjustment for workers in the industry may well result from the removal of quota controls. We are, therefore, adopting a pro-active approach to anticipated challenges. Rather than react with band-aid measures after the fact, we are proposing a strategy which recognizes the particular dynamics of the industry. Altogether, the footwear industry comprises approximately 175 companies and employs 15,000 workers. Most companies are fairly small, with an average of 86 employees.
To assist those affected, the Government has planned a three-pronged attack. We will provide aid to companies, to communities and to individual workers in the footwear industry.
Companies anticipating human resource problems can go to the Government's industrial adjustment service which can make available up to $100,000 on a cost-shared basis for a variety of purposes, including joint research into alternate business proposals and the adjustment needs of employees who might become vulnerable to market forces.
Employees are also eligible for the Government's skill investment and skill shortages programs for professional retraining and will bring into play the Labour Adjustment Benefits Program to assist older workers unable to take advantage of new job opportunities.
A further level of assistance will be applied when disruption in footwear employment might affect a whole community. Affected communities can take advantage of the industrial adjustment service on much the same terms as affected companies. In addition, the Community Futures Program will be well placed to provide direct assistance to communities which have been dependent on the footwear industry. This assistance will come in the form of program options designed to encourage new enterpreneurial activity and new employment or, if necessary, helping workers to relocate.
These are programs with a high degree of flexibility. We are confident that they will enable us to promote the Canadian footwear industry's growing ability to compete, both at home and in international markets, and to do so without causing great upheaval in the lives of Canadians employed in the footwear industry.	.
If we have learned anything from the past decade, Mr. Speaker, it is that the real source of our wealth is the ingenuity, the intelligence and the hard work of the Canadian people. However, we have also learned that if we are to preserve our wealth and increase it, we must be competitive at home and abroad and that if we are to be competitive we cannot impede change but must embrace it. One year ago the agenda for economic renewal summed up the challenge in one sentence. It said: "The art of progress is to preserve order amid change and to preserve change amid order". That, Mr. Speaker, is the intention of the action I am announcing today.

subsubtopic: FOOTWEAR IMPORT QUOTAS-STATEMENT OF MINISTER FOR INTERNATIONAL TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to quote what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in Sherbrooke in August 1984. As reported in the newspaper La Tribune, the Prime Minister stated: "The policy on quotas will be maintained". He also said he was not in favour of free trade in that sector. He went on to say "he would not give in even under pressure which might come from European Common Market countries, the United States, and other nations".

November 20, 1985

November 20, 1985

What a cruel lie, Mr. Speaker, what a cruel lie! Today the Prime Minister has betrayed the Sherbrooke footwear workers as well as all other footwear workers in Canada.
Footwear workers can now call the Prime Minister the Pinocchio of Sherbrooke. Does he not feel any shame?

We have seen today one more in a long, long list of broken promises by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). During the election campaign he said, with brave words of assurance to the people of the Eastern Townships, the people of Quebec and Ontario, that he was not going to succumb to the pressures of those other countries, that he would protect their industries and keep the quotas on. Today we hear his Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) trying to put a gloss on those words and trying to bury them in the deep ground of shame which has covered the Government since it took office. Members of the Government have no intention of living up to their commitments and promises. They make a mockery of the profession of public service by completely and totally contradicting any sense of trust or confidence that people placed in them. It was not us who said that, Mr. Speaker. It was the present Prime Minister who made those declarations. Presumably he made them with some intention of carrying them out. Presumably, as a man of honour, which he likes to claim he is, he did not use those words lightly. He used them with great seriousness and great gravity because he knows how important that industry is to the people of those regions. Surely, Mr. Speaker, there is not a nose cover large enough in Canada to provide any camouflage for the kind of treason that the Government commits day after day as it breaks promise after promise.
Something that is perhaps even more serious than that broken promise, as serious as that may be, is what it tells us about the future. Since September 24 we have been trying to debate in this House the commitments that the Government is making to all kinds of other workers about what it will do when it negotiates trade. The Government says that it is going to protect the cultural industries and workers in agriculture, in the auto pact and in the lumber industry. The Government says that we should trust and believe it because it never changes its mind but is firm and determined. Mr. Speaker, I would ask members of the Government to today talk to workers in the shoe industry in Canada to find out how much they believe the Government and how much confidence we can entrust in these negotiations.
The very time when someone else calls the tune, our song and dance man is up on his toes whistling Dixie. That is the problem with our Prime Minister. We cannot believe what he has to say. As we enter into perhaps the most serious negotiations on trade in the history of the country we are faced with this example of betrayal and broken promises. That is the foundation upon which we are supposed to build the new regime of international commerce. That is what the Government is asking Canadians to place their trust in. Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is a serious and grave indictment and creates an
Statements by Ministers
incredible sense of uncertainty on the part of all Canadians as we make this leap of faith which we are being asked to do.
The fact of the matter, Mr. Speaker, is that the Government does not have a comprehensive, clear approach to the issue of trade. It does not understand that a trade policy is an extension of domestic economic reality. The Government treats it as a form of abstract economic theology which, since it was implanted in the agenda for economic renewal, takes on the appearance of being cast in stone. It has now become sacrosanct, another sacred trust. The Government does not understand that a trade policy should be the means to an end. It should be the way of securing employment. In order to develop a proper and effective trade policy one has to integrate and bring together problems of labour markets, capitalization, modernization and export-import policies. Sector by sector there must be a series of Government actions of consultation, planning and development to make sure that that sector is prepared to face whatever international competition exists.
The Minister said that we must live by international trade. We do not disagree. We agree that as a country we must broaden our markets and secure better markets. However, in order to achieve that we must have strong Canadian industries. We must have productivity, growth and competition at home in order to allow our industries to compete abroad. Surely that is the example set by Japen, which is presently probably the world's greatest exporting nation. It does not open its doors wide and say: "Come on in". Japan protects its fledgling industries. It gives old industries protection until they can regroup, remodernize and refresh themselves and then they compete abroad. That is the plan of attack of the Japanese rather than this theological abstraction which we get from the Government on the other side. The Government does not understand that, Mr. Speaker. It says that the eight years which the shoe industry has had is long enough.
Notice the inherent contradiction in the Minister's own statement. He says that protection is no good. Then, two paragraphs later, he goes on to admit that during that period of protection the industry has made a successful effort to start its modernization, to start retooling, the start bringing in new equipment and to start developing new markets. In other words, it has used that period to begin rebuilding itself for a new day. However, the industry has said very clearly that as yet, it has not had enough time; it has not achieved the point where it can meet that competition. During the period when there was a quota protection the industry did start turning itself around and rebuilding for the future. Now the Government has cut it off at the knees. It has short-circuited and short changed that industry.
You do not have to take my word for it, Mr. Speaker. I will quote the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), the colleague of the Minister of International Trade. In giving the declaration of his new philosophy of economic regional development to the Financial Times he said: "A country like Canada may have to say we want to be free as far as our trading relationships are concerned. But it's got to be in the context of saying there is a portion of the market that we

November 20, 1985
Statements by Ministers
should reserve for Canadian companies". That was the statement of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion.
Where is that statement contained in the report of the Minister of International Trade? I did not see any reference to the statement of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion that he was going to protect a portion of every industry for Canadian production. The poor Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, he takes a few weeks off because of a severe illness and his colleagues totally and completely abandon his policies. He is betrayed, as are the workers in the shoe industry, because his so-called new approach to economic development has just been torn to shreds. Even worse, we on this side of the House find it absolutely incredible to accept that at the very time when we must strengthen and modernize the industry, the Government has discarded the one program that was enabling the shoe and textile industries to rebuild themselves. Two years ago, we formed the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board, a Government agency the decisions of which were made by senior executives from the private sector. The Chairman of the Board was Mr. Desmarais from Power Corporation and he was helped by union and business people from across Canada.
The import tribunal itself in its own report gives substantial credit to CIRB for having been the catalyst that was enabling the shoe industry to begin to bring in new machinery and develop new techniques. What did the Government do? It got rid of the program. It is cancelling it and has stopped its funding. It abandons it. While there was one real way in which the Government of Canada could help the industry to develop and modernize, the Government, in all its wisdom, gets rid of the program. That is really smart. That shows a great comprehension of industrial strategy. That shows that the Government knows what it is doing.
I recall that when we attended the meeting of the Canada-U.S. Parliamentary Association, a Member from Quebec applauded the wonderful job CIRB was doing while the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was getting rid of it.

The Minister says that we must be prepared to change and to progress. Change should not mean chaos. subsubtopic: FOOTWEAR IMPORT QUOTAS-STATEMENT OF MINISTER FOR INTERNATIONAL TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) has made a statement today. It is a statement which has to be characterized, I believe, as sad, uncreative and unjust. It is a statement that in fact abandons 20,000 workers, breaks a major promise and will lead to a gross waste of the restructuring help which we have already committed to this industry.
What is worse, Mr. Speaker, is that this statement comes at entirely the wrong time. It comes at a time when the United States is toughening up its demands and its bargaining position prior to crucial negotiations that will take place between our two countries. While we are giving away gifts, giving up ground and abandoning positions by backing off from our quotas on the shoe industry and refusing to put Canadian-content rules into effect for a company like Hyundai, the United States is playing hardball. It is being tough. It is putting its position up front as strongly as possible so that when we sit down at the bargaining table, the United States will feel good and it will feel as if it had built a strong offensive position. We will have given up so much ground that we will be weaker than we need to be. We will face those negotiations with weakness instead of strength.
Statements by Ministers
Mr. Speaker, we need a strong trade strategy, but this Government makes gifts to the Americans before the negotiations. We have had the case of Hyundai in the automobile industry and we now see what is happening to the shoe industry. The Americans are not taking the same approach; they are making even more demands. However, the strategy of this Conservative Government is to make more gifts instead of increasing its demands.
Last year, Mr. Speaker, Canadian men and women chose a new Government because they wanted a new policy. What the voters wanted most of all was a human Government, but the Minister said in his speech: "We see no reason to reject the conclusions contained in the report of the Tribunal." As for us, Mr. Speaker, we can see 20,000 such reasons, namely the workers of the shoe industry who could lose their jobs because of this decision. If the Minister and the Government have read this document carefully, they will know that it contains very important points showing the need for a specific decision which is not the one made by the Minister. For instance, Mr. Speaker, we can read the following on page 67:
The upheavals caused by this readjustment mechanism will certainly be significant for the businesses and workers directly involved.
We also find the following on page 66:
The manufacturers viewed as particularly vulnerable are the small manufacturers located mostly in Montreal, the small manufacturers in Quebec outside Montreal, and perhaps even those in Toronto, who may also be threatened.
This is a fact, Mr. Speaker, and it is a fact that the Prime Minister knew before the elections. At the time, the Prime Minister said that we needed these quotas for the shoe industry. But, Mr. Speaker, now that he is Prime Minister, he says: "It is not necessary, we do not want to do that." For all the voters in Quebec and Canada, that is the problem with our Government. Many Canadians voted for this Government because the Prime Minister had said before the election that we needed those quotas. However, after the election, in spite of his promises, he had decided to scrap that policy.

There is no question that there are serious challenges which face the country in dealing with industries such as the shoe industry, the textile industry, the electrical products industry and many of the other industries which face competition from low wage countries throughout the world. It is a touch challenge, but the answer to it is not to abandon these industries to their own fate. It is not to bow in hollow supplication to past economic theories. The challenge is not to surrender the shoe industry because we want to prove to the Americans that we are really committed to free trade. The challenge is to lead an industry to adjust, adopt restructure, modernize and change in order to face the competition of the future.
That is the challenge which the country has faced dismally. It is a challenge which was faced more by the previous

November 20, 1985
Statements by Ministers
Government than by the present Government. The failure to respond effectively to that challenge lies particularly with the previous Government. The Minister of International Trade is quite right to say that quotas which have been in place for eight years should have done their job by now. The fact of the matter is that because of the failure of the past Government's strategy this industry did not adjust, did not adapt and did not begin to modernize until far too late. If the Minister had taken the time to examine the case, I think he probably would have seen this.
I must say that I was particularly struck to hear my colleague from the Liberal Party speak about how he viewed adjustment policy as helping companies pack their bags in communities and give up their future. That is not how we view restructuring policy. We see the strategy which we have to take toward these sectors as a creative one in order to help them prepare for the future so that they can compete successfully. However, the present tribunal report fully documents the failure of our past policy.
I would like to read again to Members of the House some quotations from that document. I quote from page 53 of the footwear report. It reads:
In its 1981 report-
This is four years after quotas were first put in place.
-the Tribunal noted that there was no indication that major restructuring had taken place since quotas were imposed.
So as of now, we face a situation where, as the tribunal itself admitted, and I quote from page 19 of the report:
The footwear industry has not yet completed this process of improvement in management efficiency ...
Let me quote perhaps the most damning statements which come from the report of the tribunal. This is the most damning judgment on past footwear policy in this country. I quote from page 100 of the report as follows:
As of October 31, 1984, roughly $14.1 million of the $17 million earmarked for footwear under CIRB's Sector Firms Program had been committed ... As of December, 1984, however, it appeared that actual payments to the footwear industry under this part of the program were in the region of only about $2.2 million.
So less than one seventh of the money allocated to help this industry modernize had actually been spent at the start of this year. That is why the decision to terminate these quotas at this stage is economic nonsense.
There are those persons within this country who take the approach of neoclassical economists to the sector. They say, "Look, we should not provide support for a sector like this which is weak and vulnerable". That is an inhuman decision. It is an inhuman approach to industrial policy. But the approach which the Government is taking is not just inhuman, it is incompetent, because it runs the very real risk of wasting the whole of $15 million which has been been allocated to help this industry and has not, as of the start of this year, yet been spent.
In my misbegotten past, I worked-I must tell the House- as an economist on these questions of restructuring. I can tell Hon. Members, on the basis of all of the work I have had a chance to do in my own research, that we cannot restructure an industry quickly. It takes time and commitment and a sense of understanding of the human problem. That is what the Government is abandoning with this approach.
This policy is not wrong because it wants to see an end to quotas. No one in this country wants to keep quotas in place forever in the footwear industry. But it is wrong because we have finally started the process of restructuring-too late, 1 agree, but we started it. Now is the chance to put this industry back on its feet, to give it a future, and to give the communities across this country who depend on this industry, the thousands of workers, the future they deserve. We need to do that not just for the sake of those workers but for the sake of our country as we enter these crucial trade negotiations so that we look like tough bargainers who are committed to jobs in this country, not to the loss of jobs to the United States.

The House resumed from Tuesday, November 19, 1985, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-49, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (prostitution), be read the third time and passed.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to resume debate on Bill C-49 and again express my disappointment with this Bill.
I may add that women's groups in particular were very disappointed.
The National Association of Women and the Law is alarmed at the content and impact of provisional measures aimed at reducing the inconvenience to the public caused by street soliciting.
The prohibiting of any communication, as proposed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie), constitutes a serious and unjustified infringement of our civil liberties, considering the respect Canadians have for freedom of speech and association and for individual freedom and security, as enshrined in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
According to the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, Bill C-49 is trying to deal with the problem of street prostitution piecemeal, without considering the economic and social climate that fosters this phenomenon. Furthermore, the Bill fails to suggest any legitimate venue where prostitution may take place, thereby increasing the risk of violence for prostitutes.
When the Minister of Justice presented his Bill in committee and we mentioned the risk of violence for prostitutes, and also that the Bill went far beyond street soliciting as such, his answer was that once the prostitutes were banned from the streets, they might have more trouble finding customers but that really was no concern of his.
It is therefore not surprising to find this kind of legislation before the House, since we have the impression that the Minister himself is not terribly concerned about what enforcement of this legislation will do.
Hj

November 20, 1985

The National Advisory Council on the Status of Women feels that Bill C-49 is unimaginative, narrow and punitive. According to the president, who was appointed by the Progressive Conservative Government, the Bill deals with only half of the problem. The CACSW believes that, although it might allay the grave concern of residents, the new legislation might force prostitutes to operate secretely, compel them to resort more often to pimps, and make them liable to more fines and jail sentences, with police records. This would restrict even further any possibility of abandoning their trade.
During committee proceedings we tried to introduce amendments about pimps-let it be said, Mr. Speaker, that there is not a single reference to pimps in this Bill-but we were told not to worry, that pimps can be arrested, that they are covered under some other legislative provisions. Yet when we ask the police why they never manage to arrest a pimp they tell us that the legislation is so badly drafted and so complicated that their hands are tied.
I entertain serious reservations about this Bill, since it covers juvenile prostitution and it will make it quite impossible to arrest pimps who will be selling the services of 12-year-old children and adult prostitutes alike. We did propose amendments but they were all turned down.
As to the client, I must admit he is mentioned in the Bill. But they have taken a very paternalistic approach in the written text given to us by the Minister of Justice. We have to wonder how the police will be able to apply the provisions of such a Bill.
I, for one, believe that we should not concern ourselves with what might go on between adults. However, since the Bill stipulates that adult prostitutes will be arrested, then clients have to be arrested as well.
If we take a closer look at what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) wrote about the clients, and 1 quote: "Most clients however have undoubtedly never been in trouble with the law . . .", those clients will indeed run the risk of ending up with a police record, besides being sentenced for having committed an infraction and publicly unveiling before the courts an aspect of their private life which is generally unknown. So I wonder if the police will be able to punish clients as they do prostitutes because even today the police tell us: We arrest the clients, but they always manage to go scot-free through the back door. In my judgement, this Bill has no teeth when it comes to the clients.
Another thing is that, throughout the debate on Bill C-49,1 expressed my concern about juvenile prostitution. I believe that making prostitutes under 18 subject to the same laws as prostitutes over 18 is fundamentally wrong. In the legislative committee, I proposed a series of amendments concerning juvenile prostitution, which my Conservative colleagues rushed to vote down.
Criminal Code
Mr. Speaker, three possibilities are generally considered when we are talking about prostitution: criminalization, legislation and decriminalization. Bill C-49, the intent of which is to wipe out street soliciting for the purpose of engaging in prostitution, tackles the first approach: criminalization. The purpose of the Bill is to give the law teeth so that it will be easier to arrest a person who is soliciting. When the Police chiefs of Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver came to testify before the Committee, they said that they liked the Bill this way, and when we discussed again how difficult it was to arrest a pimp who was selling the services of an adolescent, the Mayor of Niagara answered: "Listen, is the Hon. Member anxious to legislate morality?" So I do not know whether it is concern for morality to want to arrest someone who is selling the services of a 10 or 12 year old child, because if Bill C-49 is enacted, it will then be possible to be arrested if a police officer sees you communicating in any way with another person, if the officer believes that such communication is for the purpose of engaging in prostitution.
Mr. Speaker, like the Law Reform Commission, 1 believe that the Criminal Code should not be used unless other means of control in our society are inadequate or inappropriate, and when rights and freedoms are threatened. 1 would say that prostitution does not threaten rights and freedoms. It may shock some people, one may find it immoral, indecent or unworthy-that is a matter of personal opinion-but prostitution does not in any way threaten the rights and freedoms of Canadians.
And if we look at prostitution as the only opportunity for individuals whose training and labour market experience are practically nil, I believe that the answers we are looking for are not judicial but social.
The Special Committee on Pornography and Prostitution, also known as the Fraser Committee, pointed out, and rightly so, that prostitution is related to lack of social and educational programs that would help young people approach confidently and responsibly the problems of sexism, sexuality and sexual identity. It is most significant that the first recommendation of the Fraser Committee on Prostitution calls upon the Government to intensify its moral and financial commitment to eliminate economic and social disparities between the sexes as well as discrimination based on sexual orientation. It is my view that any legislation on prostitution should contain social provision aimed at eradicating the causes of prostitution that relate to social and economic injustice. The Fraser and Badgley Reports are replete with all kinds of proposals to that effect. They deal among other things with social programs aimed at women and young children in need, with sexual education programs to be implemented in schools, with assistance to community groups contributing to the welfare of present and former prostitutes, so that they may have access to social, health, employment and educational services.

November 20, 1985
Criminal Code
The studies, the research, have been made, the special committees have been set up, and we now have a set of realistic recommendations available. All that is now lacking for action across the board is the political will.
And when I heard the Minister of Justice suggest yesterday that this legislation was not a response to the Badgley and Fraser Reports, that we would have another legislation in early 1986, I was somewhat concerned because looking at the current approach and the current Bill on prostitution, we have cause to wonder whether the Government would ever have a better approach to juvenile prostitution. 1 am therefore sorry that such a legislation should be allowed to pass, and it is my hope that a more specific remedy will be forthcoming concerning juvenile prostitution.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on third reading of Bill C-49 to reiterate the strong opposition of the federal New Democratic Party to this legislation. Having heard from a number of witnesses that appeared before the legislative committee considering Bill C-49, certainly our position has, if anything, been strengthened and reinforced.
The Bill is a sweeping attack on civil liberties. The approach which is taken in this legislation is fundamentally misguided. The Bill is dangerous and will merely drive prostitution underground in the short run. It will make prostitutes more subject to violence, more dependent on pimps, or it will mean that prostitutes who return to the streets after having been charged will run more often. This was indicated by a woman who appeared before the committee. She is presently working the streets of Vancouver as a prostitute.
We were told that the effect of the Bill will be to create a revolving door. Prostitutes will be arrested and charged. They will pay the fine and return to the street to work in order to pay off their fine. Indeed, the representative of the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police who appeared before the committee agreed that it was likely that the Bill would not significantly affect the number of prostitutes working on the streets. The association recognized that the prostitutes would likely be back on the streets. It said that that is why it would pursue the customers of prostitutes.
I asked the representatives of the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, when they appeared before the committee, how the police intend to go after the customers of the prostitutes. They said that they will use undercover female officers to arrest the customers. I then asked how many female officers are working in the morality squads of the Vancouver police department, the Toronto police department, the Montreal police department or the Niagara Falls police department. Across Canada there are perhaps eight or ten women who are working in those positions within the police departments. The reality is that women will not be in a position to be used as undercover police personnel to arrest male customers. 1 asked the chiefs of police if they had an alternative plan for pursuing the customers. They said that they could use boom microphones to intercept communications between prostitutes and customers. I suggest that those who enforce our laws should also read them because using boom microphones to interrupt communications between Canadians is illegal under the provisions of the Criminal Code. I would hope that the police of this land would not be using illegal techniques in order to attempt to make arrests under the provisions of Bill C-49. When I pressed the police, Mr. Speaker, and asked, if boom microphones were not allowed and that if there were not enough female undercover personnel, what techniques they would use to go after customers, they said: "Well, that is classified information. We are not prepared to tell you".
The reason the police are not prepared to tell us is that this Bill will be applied overwhelmingly against the poorest of prostitutes, against prostitutes who work on the streets. It will not affect the call-girls, those who service the economic elite in our society, the doctors, the lawyers and the wealthy. No, Mr. Speaker, it will touch the poorest of the poor, the women who are huddled under street lamps in order to prostitute themselves. Surely that is the real question.
Why is it that women, and in some cases men, are selling their bodies as commodities on the street, Mr. Speaker? As the Fraser Commission has documented very clearly, this is fundamentally an economic and social problem. To deal with an economic and social problem using harsh and repressive criminal measures is profoundly mistaken.
I would argue that certainly those who live in residential communities, whether they be in Vancouver in the Mount Pleasant area or in the west end of Vancouver or Toronto, Montreal, Halifax and elsewhere, have a right to live in peace and quiet. Their children have a right to go to school without being harassed. People have a right to sleep at night without hearing the screeching of tires and obscenities being hurled underneath their windows.
We must ask, before adopting the Draconian provisions of Bill C-49, have the police exhausted all other possibilities? I suggest that the answer to that question is no, they have not. In fact, the police should not be coming before Parliament seeking these sweeping new remedies without being able to demonstrate clearly that they have attempted to use other provisions, other sections of the Criminal Code, including Section 171 dealing with disorderly conduct, Section 169, concerning indecent acts and sections concerning assault.
Carefully drafted municipal by-laws concerning traffic, noise and nuisance can be enacted or enforced locally to aid in the control of nuisance factors that are associated with street prostitution. Indeed, a by-law has been upheld in Montreal that effectively regulates the nuisance aspects of street prostitution.
My colleagues, particularly the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) and my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), recognize and are deeply concerned about the serious problem of street prostitution in residential communities.
November 20, 1985

We have before us a piece of legislation which does not just deal with street soliciting, but it goes far beyond that, representing a sweeping attack on freedom of expression in Canada. I say that because while the Government says it wants this Bill to deal with street soliciting, the Bill does not just deal with street soliciting. It deals in its very terms with any form of communication or attempted communication in any public place anywhere in Canada. That, Mr. Speaker, is not just streets. It is nightclubs, bars, inside automobiles, anywhere to which the public has access as of right or by invitation.
When the Canadian Civil Liberties Association appeared before our committee, it pointed out that these provisions were Draconian. They go far beyond what the chiefs of police sought to deal with street prostitution. The association pointed out some of the behaviour which would be illegal under the provisions of this Bill.
Under this Bill it would be unlawful for a passenger in a taxi to ask a driver how to contact a prostitute. It would be unlawful for a hotel guest in an elevator to ask such questions of a bellhop or for a customer to ask it of his pharmacist in a drugstore, no matter how inconspicuous or discreet such communications might be. In fact, there are no limitations whatever in this Bill in the scope of it in terms of communication. A wink, a nod, a smile could trigger a criminal prosecution. I suggest that such provisions may very well be struck down under the provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
What we are told is to trust the police, that they will not abuse the sweeping new powers we are giving them. Sure, we may be giving them a little more than they asked for, but we should trust them; they will not abuse the powers. I suggest that we do not give powerful new weapons to the police and then suggest that perhaps if we have given them too much power, having a sunset clause in the Bill would allow us three years later to remove those powers. That is an abrogation of our responsibility as Members of Parliament to draft legislation with thought and care by giving power that go well beyond those which should be accorded to the police.
What about the manner in which this Bill deals with kids on the street, young people, juveniles? One area of consensus on the Justice Committee in 1983 was that in dealing with the problem of juvenile prostitution, one should not make criminals out of young people. Surely one must go after the customer of the young person and nail the customer.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) who sat on the committee at that time was in full agreement, and indeed the entire NDP caucus urged the Government to act on that recommendation with respect to juvenile prostitution. What is there in Bill C-49 to deal with the question of juvenile prostitution, Mr. Speaker?
What this Bill does is to label young people who engage in prostitution as criminals. It would give them a record and drive them further underground and make much more difficult attempts to try to use social and economic programs to get them off the street.
Criminal Code
When I asked the chiefs of police what they intended to do with the kids they arrest as criminals, they said: "We recognize that there are not adequate programs available". The Province of British Columbia, the province from which I come, has totally inadequate programs to assist young people in getting off the street. The Chief of Police for Vancouver said: "We know there are not programs now but when this Bill is passed, we trust there will be additional pressure put on the Government to bring in programs to deal with young people". That is nonsense. Certainly the provincial Government of British Columbia has been cutting back on social programs. What we will see is young people who are engaged in prostitution again back on the streets or going underground, even more dependent on pimps.
The Bill fails to deal with the reality of juvenile prostitution and to recognize that in some cases, particularly in the case of young men, they are on the street because there continues to be discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in Canada, and that violence and repression in their own communities, particularly in small towns, drives them to the street which is the only place where they get any kind of acceptance. That is one of the reasons the subcommittee on equality rights was unanimous in its strong recommendation calling for a legislative amendment to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in Canada.
The Bill would sweep the streets of prostitution according to the police, but what it fails to recognize is that prostitution itself is not illegal in Canada today, and that in sweeping prostitution from the streets and doing nothing to deal with bawdy house laws the Government, in effect, is providing no alternative.
The Fraser Commission was clear in its denunciation of that kind of proposal. It indicated the following:
We see no virtue in replacing the present system with a more repressive regime. There is no evidence in the history of this country or those countries like the United States which retain a Draconian system, that the results of such an approach would justify it. Indeed, we are inclined to think that a move in that direction would subvert any attempt to treat prostitution sensitively as a major social problem.
A major social problem and a major economic problem it is. I should like to refer to a letter which I received from a gentleman in Vancouver, a representative of the Evangelical Tabernacle in that city. He has been involved in helping prostitutes by Christian street witnessing. After a year of this work, he became a volunteer worker at a drop-in centre for prostitutes. He said that Bill C-49 would legislate prostitutes underground, resulting in more pimps and more violence to the prostitutes. Also he said that working bars would force prostitutes to pay off both bartenders and doormen, and that there would be more involvement of organized crime. Also he noted that women who are prostitutes today, for the most part, do not want to live that way.
We heard evidence from a prostitute who appeared before the committee which indicated that some prostitutes chose prostitution as a job. Certainly many of us find it difficult to

understand prostitution as a career choice, but I think it should be noted in this debate that there are those who choose it as a job. The vast majority of those who work as prostitutes were either violently abused or sexually abused as children. Also many of them are involved in prostitution because they are poor and are on welfare. Prostitution is a way of feeding their children.
In the Province of Quebec, young people under the age of 30 years and on welfare are supposed to survive on $161 per month. Is it any wonder that some of those young kids are on the streets when that is the amount of income they receive? In the Province of British Columbia, an individual with one child is supposed to survive on $640 per month. As the individual to whom I referred earlier stated, the best way to clear the streets of prostitution is to raise the welfare rates.
In conclusion, in that I know my 20 minutes are up, again I emphasize a very strong opposition to the approach taken in this legislation. Also I want to emphasize that the Government is attempting to deal with what is fundamentally a social and economic problem by using a legal sledge-hammer. That approach is profoundly wrong.
I hope the Government comes forward early in the new year with recommendations to deal with some of the suggestions of the Fraser Commission. We are by no means adopting those recommendations holus-bolus. After very careful study, the commission made a number of recommendations in respect of changes to bawdy house laws and in respect of decriminalization, which I think the House would be wise to adopt.
Finally, as a Parliament, we are engaged today, in many ways, in what is an act of collective hypocrisy. We can go to sleep tonight, suggesting that we have dealt in a serious way with the problem of prostitution; we have swept our streets clean of the poorest prostitutes. Until we come to grips with the social and economic reasons for prostitution, the second-class status of women in society, economically and socially, until we put more resources into dealing with violence against women, we will be continuing to adopt a piecemeal, destructive approach which represents an attack not just on the civil rights of prostitutes but ultimately on the civil rights of Canadian men and women.
