subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this afternoon to speak on Bill C-49, an Act to amend the Criminal Code with regard to prostitution. An extremely heavy-handed amendment is being proposed. It lacks common sense. It will not deal with the problem of street soliciting or the nuisance problem with which Canadians want us to deal. Instead, it will result in the criminalization largely of women, young women and children.
The reason the Bill is before us is that the police have not been able to cope with the problem of street soliciting with the present means at their disposal. They have asked and lobbied very vigorously, supported by many mayors and citizens, for stronger powers. I am sympathetic with the objective of their concern because citizens are entitled to quiet neighbourhoods and a trouble-free existence in their homes, as well as going to and from them. However, the Bill will not help achieve that peace and quiet. It will raise a whole set of new problems.
The old interpretation that soliciting had to constitute pressing and persistent importuning was one which limited prosecutions on soliciting. However, there are other measures which could be used to deal with street soliciting. I sat on the Justice Committee when we examined this question and came up with a couple of much more appropriate, very concrete proposals to deal with the street problem. One was to enforce existing nuisance, noise, disorderly conduct and traffic provisions of the Criminal Code. I have discussed with police officers why these provisions are not better enforced. In fact, I recall discussing the matter with the then chief of the Toronto police who pointed out a great problem posed by street soliciting, that traffic was held up and that cars lined up as motorists were looking for prostitutes standing on the corners. He said that it was a very serious problem, and I asked him what they did about it. He said: "We arrest them". I said: "Do you mean that you arrest the motorists?" He said: "Oh, no, we don't arrest the motorists; we arrest the girls". I think this conversation points to the hypocrisy of the implementation of our current laws. The Bill before us now will not do anything to change that hypocrisy.
I should like to refer to some of the statistics on enforcement of street soliciting under our existing laws. We have no reason to believe that there will be any improvement in going after customers. Heretofore the laws have been enforced against women, and this is what we have to expect to happen. In Toronto, 78.2 per cent of the soliciting charges laid in 1979 were laid against women in 1980, 69.9 per cent; in 1981, 82.6 per cent; and in 1982, 80.8 per cent. This is a law which is enforced against women. The idea that it will be enforced against customers, male customers in most cases, is absolutely ludicrous. We know that it will not happen. We know what are the enforcement procedures. The police have enforced it against customers to a very limited extent. Referring to the loitering charges in Toronto, 84.5 per cent were laid against women; charges laid under counselling to commit an indecent act, 67.2 per cent were against women.
In the case of Vancouver, 65 per cent of the charges were laid against female prostitutes. The vast majority of charges are in fact being laid against women, not against customers. In Halifax, 77.8 per cent were laid against women. In the case of British Columbia there is an anomoly that customers cannot be charged under the Criminal Code. They could be charged under by-laws, but not under the Criminal Code as a result of a most unfortunate interpretation by a court which was never appealed. Of course the answer to that is to change the law to close that loophole. That would have been, by far, the more
November 20, 1985

appropriate thing to do, to make it possible to charge more customers and in fact go ahead and do that when there is a genuine problem of street soliciting.
I have referred to the 1983 Justice Committee report which made a very important recommendation which 1 supported very strongly. It recommended that it be an offence for an adult to ask for or agree to pay for an act of prostitution with a minor. We know that there are large numbers of young people on the streets and it should certainly be up to adults who are seeking prostitutes to ensure that they do not seek an act of prostitution from a minor. It seems to me that adult behaviour requires a certain amount of responsibility and it would be far better to put the onus on improving adult behaviour to save young people this experience. Yet, the Bill before us today does not do that. There was strong support from the Justice Committee for that very concrete and direct proposal, and yet it was ignored by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) in the drafting of this new legislation.
The Bill before us today attempts to deal with the nuisance problem of street prostitution in isolation from the social and economic climate which promoted the problem in the first place. We have an unemployment rate of one in five among young people who are, in growing numbers, becoming prostitutes. We must understand that that is the problem to be dealt with and this sledge-hammer approach, this punitive approach, is not going to deal with the causes of young people going into prostitution. It provides no legal venue in which prostitution may take place. It is a damned-if-you-do, damned-if-you-don't situation. If the idea was to get it off the streets, the Bill criminalizes soliciting in other places as well.
In the testimony of the Mayor of Vancouver he said that it was not the concern of the Vancouver city council or the citizens of Vancouver to try to ban prostitution entirely. He said that that was unrealistic, it was not something that could be done, and they were not attempting to do that. They were attempting to get it off the streets and out of places in which it was a nuisance to the public who could not enjoy their homes and were hassled going to and from work and going in and out for the evening. Yet, this Bill does not meet those very reasonable expectations of the Mayor of Vancouver and city councillors. It goes far beyond that to criminalize behaviour in a much more general fashion. They suggested that we needed to get it off the streets and put it where it will not be a source of nuisance to other people.
This legislation will simply result in a large number of people being criminalized and we will get into the revolving door syndrome. There will be more dependence in pimps. Women will have to call their pimps to get bail. They will have to go back on the streets to pay their fines and lawyers' fees. This is the kind of legal control that we do not want. We have had it before. The idea is that we need tougher laws to deal with this problem. However, we used to have tougher laws. The jails of Vancouver used to be filled with prostitutes. It was a revolving door. If they could not pay their fine and no one
Criminal Code
would raise bail for them they simply stayed in. Then, when they got out, they had to get back to work to pay the rent and do all the things which people have to do. It simply got them further and further into a criminal milieu and it was harder and harder for them to get into ordinary work and out of that kind of life.
We have tried the revolving door. It was repugnant to people and they argued against it. As a result of all those arguments we had the laws improved and now the Government wants us to go backward. My Party is very strongly opposing this legislation. We are opposing the revolving door and the increased criminalization of women and young people.
If passed, this Bill would result in prostitutes being at risk of violence to a greater extent. It would increase the male exploitation of female prostitutes because they would be more dependent on people to intervene for them with the law. They will be more vulnerable as a result of this legislation. It also endangers the freedom of expression of other Canadians. The wording of Bill C-49 is very broad indeed. It says:
Every person who in a public place or in any place open to public view (c) stops or attempts to stop any person or in any manner communicates or
attempts to communicate with any person
for the purpose of engaging in prostitution or of abtaining the services of a
prostitute is guilty of an offence-
The words "stop or . . . in any manner communicates" is very general. This very, very general wording which will result in large numbers of people being criminalized is totally inappropriate and is possibly contrary to the Charter of Rights. Certainly one obvious result, if this legislation is passed, is that there will be court cases challenging the legality of the legislation instead of proceeding in a practical and focused way to deal with the immediate problem. It is aimed at the most vulnerable prostitutes, those who are young, those who are unskilled. It is an extremely repugnant measure, Mr. Speaker.
I suggest that we should take quite a different approach to this problem. We should be closing the loopholes and making it an offence to solicit an act of prostitution from a minor. We should be enforcing the laws of nuisance, disorderliness and noise, which measures are available. If I were a police chief in a city which had a prostitution problem I can assure you that there would not be a street soliciting problem. The matter could be dealt with. Police forces have sheltered and protected the male customers out of a mistaken sense of male bonding. They have gone after the prostitute, the evil woman in the case, and sheltered the male customer. They have done this out of a very mistaken sense of honour saying that they are only innocent occasional offenders whose reputations should not be harmed by having it known.
In no jurisdiction in Canada has there been public reporting of the names of offenders who have been customers in cases of soliciting. The furthest that has been gone in this direction was in Vancouver and I will tell you how paltry the measures were. Male customers were reported using their surnames and initials only with no addresses. For example: "R. Smith was convicted of an act of street soliciting". Obviously that is no risk to the reputation of anyone. It is the customer who can be

November 20, 1985
Criminal Code
controlled by the threat of loss of reputation. Clearly, for the prostitute the publication of a name is neither here nor there. Indeed, it might be advertising. However, the customer has something to lose. Yes, this very obvious method of dealing with the problem has not been used. Police forces would rather use the sledge-hammer than use the very practical tactic of publishing the names of offenders who are customers. If 1 were a police chief I would use this cheap, easy and convenient means of clearing up the problem. I would not wish to resort to this far more heavy-handed, extremely expensive measure. It is expensive in terms of prison costs and in terms of the human costs for people who are going to suffer very much as a result.
A large number of people spoke very strongly at committee stage in opposition to this Bill. A large number of women's organizations made representations. The National Action Committee on the Status of Women spoke very strongly. It gave a brief detailing the reprehensible nature of the proposed measures and proposing a very different approach. They recommend a much more global approach which understands the social and economic context in which street soliciting occurs. The Elizabeth Fry Society, an organization which I belong to and support, has been very strong in support of the rehabilitation of women offenders and in support of civil liberties in a general fashion. The members of this organization work directly with women offenders, including women prostitutes, and they are very familiar with the problem. Their advice ought to have been heeded rather than this more Draconian approach which the Conservative Government approves.
I will quote from the position taken by representatives of the Elizabeth Fry Society before the Justice Committee. They
said:
Our goal is to ensure that prostitutes have alternatives to selling their bodies in order to make a living. Criminal records decrease this likelihood and further demoralize people who are already condemned by many sectors of our society. Criminalizing prostitution and/or soliciting expresses public condemnation of women who, if anything, are closer to victims than to criminals ... Criminalizing soliciting in fact increases the prostitute's dependency on her pimp. She needs him for protection, and she has no means of protecting herself from the pimp. She will have to work the streets even harder and be more persistent in her soliciting to repay her pimp for the trouble she has caused him.
Again, does this measure deal with the problems caused by pimps? Not at all. We have heard plenty of testimony from women's organizations indicating that we should throw the book at pimps. That is a difficult thing to do. I am sympathetic to police forces which point out the difficulties of dealing with pimps. However, how hard have they tried? Pimps are the people who really cause problems. Indeed, one of the revelations of the Badgley Commission was that young people who were prostitutes and solicited in a pressing and persistent manner did so as a result of orders from their pimps who said that they were not making enough money. It was the pimps who were creating the problem, not the prostitutes themselves. Yet this measure will not do anything about the problems posed by pimps.
Let me continue to quote from testimony of representatives of the Elizabeth Fry Society:
-prostitutes generally are not dangerous criminals; they are not people who we would wish, on an objective test, to put into our prisons, particularly at a time when the provincial prisons across this country are, I believe without exception, overcrowded, particularly the remand and short sentence centres. 1 am wondering whether we really want to increase the double and triple bunking in our prisons, particularly with young people-many of the prostitutes are young people; an increasing number are juveniles as well. These, I believe, really are not appropriately dealt with through toughening of the Criminal Code.
Another proposal was made by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women as follows:
It would seem a far better use of government funds to support women in retraining programs, and provide street workers and alternate living quarters away from the street, than to spend funds on policing, court costs, and imprisonment of prostitutes.
I have raised a few points on the question of policing. Let me continue with some further analyses that the police themselves have revealed. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) has pointed officers who could act as undercover officers to entrap male customers. There is a much larger number of male police officers ready and apparently quite willing to work in this capacity to attract women prostitutes. This was the historic way of getting conviction quotas up when the old laws were in force and many more women were going to prison than is the case now.
I recall asking the Chief of Police of Toronto about this matter. I asked him why he did not go after the customers and one of the answers he gave me was that he did not have many women police officers and they did not like doing it. Women police officers do not like enforcing a law using entrapment. I asked the Chief of Police about the situation with men police officers and he told me that they do not mind so much. That is a double standard. We should not be happy about it. Yet that is the nature of the beast. We must understand this and we should have laws which will take us away from the double standard. We must be very sensitive to the fact that this is a law that will really be used against women and children and that it is entirely inappropriate.
To conclude, let me say that this is not a law that will do any good. It will not stop the problem of street soliciting. It will not deal with the problem of children on the streets. It will criminalize a large number of people and will increase dependence on pimps. It will worsen the situation of children on the streets. This is a heavy-handed, Draconian measure and it lacks common sense. It is an irresponsible measure and I urge the House to defeat Bill C-49.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments? If not, we will resume debate.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak to Bill C-49. Put very simply, Bill C-49 is not the answer to the problem.
It was hoped that after committee deliberations over this Bill, the Government would recognize that the Bill was offensive and deserving of substantial amendment. Be that as it may, the Government, in its wisdom, decided not to amend the
November 20, 1985

Bill. It decided to bring the Bill before the House for third reading with no amendments other than the inclusion of one word in the first clause.
In my respectful submission, the Bill is not supportable simply from a civil libertarian point of view. There is no question that the Bill poses a threat to individual rights and freedoms and we as Parliamentarians must be the custodians of civil liberties and of individual rights and freedoms. We must ensure that in our deliberations, we afford as much protection as possible to Canadians so that we may protect those rights.
In my submission, I would like to indicate why this Bill is not deserving of support from a civil libertarian point of view. However, I would like to begin by indicating why we are here today debating Bill C-49. In my view, the Bill is a knee-jerk political reaction to a problem that does exist. We recognize that the problem of street prostitution does exist. It is a nuisance in many of the major cities of Canada including Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto, Halifax and others. However, Bill C-49 is not the answer.
We argued at committee and at second reading stage that what was needed was a comprehensive piece of legislation to deal with all the aspects of and problems associated with prostitution in Canada. The Minister indicated on a number of occasions that it is the intention of the Government to bring forward a comprehensive piece of legislation as early as the new year. Why then? Why pass this Bill which is so basically and fundamentally flawed now?
In my view, this Bill will be struck down by the courts. You can bet your bottom dollars, Mr. Speaker, that it will be challenged at the earliest opportunity. I am confident that a superior court will strike this Bill down as being too vague and not specific enough.
The Government decided that it had to act because of political pressure. As you are well aware, Mr. Speaker, when Governments act under political pressure, they make bad laws at times. This one is a bad law.
We know that the Criminal Code has not been effective in dealing with the problem of street prostitution. We had Section 195.1 of the Criminal Code of Canada which reads:
Every person who solicits any person in a public place for the purpose of prostitution is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
The courts of the land have interpreted that particular Section as stated in a Supreme Court of Canada decision as meaning that the activity had to be pressing and persistent. A mere wink, a wave or a mere communication was not sufficient to prosecute and convict under the particular section. The police forces across the land felt fettered as a result of that particular Supreme Court of Canada decision. The previous administration decided that the whole question of prostitution had to be looked into. In that respect we had the Fraser Commission and the Badgley Commission which looked into the matter and related areas. Both Commissions have tabled reports in the House of Commons and both have made recommendations with respect to the problems. While all Members
Criminal Code
of the House may not support these recommendations I think it is important that the Government respond in a comprehensive way to the Fraser Report and bring in legislation which will deal with the problems associated with prostitution and with pimps. Bill C-49 does not deal with pimps, nor does it deal with common bawdy houses because of political pressure which the Government has brought to bear with respect to this legislation.
Bill C-49 is a short piece of legislation. It has but two clauses. I think it is important to point out that the Government is unsure of itself with respect to the Bill. This can be concluded by reading the two clauses contained in the Bill. One of the clauses is a sunset clause. It requires the Government of Canada to conduct a comprehensive review of the provisions of this Bill after three years. That suggests to me that the Government is not sure whether this Bill will survive and whether it is the answer. I think the Government realizes deep down inside that the Bill might not survive. I think the Government is paying a disservice to those who are concerned about the problems of street prostitution. It is doing a disservice because, as I indicated earlier with all the certainty I could command, this Bill will be challenged.
What will be the result if the Bill is challenged? It will go to a trial court and a trial judge will make a decision either in favour or against it. Regardless of the decision made someone, either the Crown or the accused, will appeal the decision to a superior court. A superior court will strike down the Bill because it is vague. Then what will happen? The police will no longer be able to act. Their hands will be tied again because the courts will deem the Bill to be unenforceable, vague and perhaps in contravention of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The legislation will be held up for months and months, if not years, before a final decision is rendered by the Supreme Court of Canada. In effect, what the Government may be doing by passing this Bill is perpetuating the problem for years to come. It may be effective on a short term basis, perhaps for a number of weeks or months. It might get the prostitutes off the streets for that period of time; but they will come back after the Supreme Court of any province decides that the Bill is unenforceable. We, as legislators, will then have to sit on our hands and wait until the Supreme Court of Canada renders a decision with respect to it. I hope the Government has thought about this aspect of the Bill and about the potential of a lengthy delay as a result of a court decision.
I would like to review the Bill and the offensive clauses in it and indicate why, in my view and in the view of many people, the Bill is not supported because it poses a threat to individual rights and freedoms. The Bill makes it an offence for any person, which would include a customer or a prostitute, who, in a public place or in any place open to public view, does one of a number of things. If that person stops or attempts to stop any motor vehicle for the purposes of engaging in prostitution or of obtaining the services of a prostitute, then that person

November 20, 1985
Criminal Code
could be prosecuted and convicted of a criminal offense. How will the courts define "stops" or "attempts to stop any motor vehicle"?
With respect to stopping a motor vehicle, it is pretty simple. If someone stands in front of a car and forces it to stop then I think it is obvious that the person is stopping a motor vehicle. However, that is not where the matter ends. The prosecution will then have to show that the person has not only stopped a motor vehicle but it will have to go on in order to secure a conviction. The prosecution must prove that the purpose of the stopping was to engage in prostitution or for obtaining the sexual services of a prostitute. How will the police be able to prove that?
I submit that there is an evidentiary problem. My friend, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), indicated some of the problems with respect to adducing such evidence in order to secure a conviction. How can that evidence be obtained? Someone will actually have to listen or understand why the vehicle is being stopped. Of course, we could use undercover police officers to this end, but there would be problems with that. Either the customer or the prostitute would have to admit or confess to the police what in effect had taken place.
Proposed Subsection 195.1(a) deals with stopping or attempting to stop any motor vehicle. What does "attempts to stop any motor vehicle" mean? It is a simple wave to the driver an attempt to stop a motor vehicle? How does one attempt to stop a motor vehicle? If one gets in the way of a motor vehicle and the driver drives around that person is that an attempt to stop a motor vehicle? One can see the problems associated with that subsection.
Let us go on to proposed Subsection 195.1(f)) which deals with the person who in a public place or in any place open to public view impedes the free flow of pedestrian or vehicular traffic or ingress to or egress from premises adjacent to that place. What does that mean? These are questions which the courts will ask. They will ask what Parliament intends when it says that it is a criminal offence to impede the free flow of pedestrian or vehicular traffic. If a prostitute or a customer simply stands on a sidewalk and someone has to side-step that person in order to get around, then is that person impeding the free flow of pedestrian traffic? That is but a judgment call. The court demand some certainty from Parliament with respect to its laws in order for those laws to be fair and in order for them to be equally applied. There is a problem with this subsection in that one does not know what it means to impede the free flow of pedestrian traffic.
1 would like to indicate at this point how it can be seen that police officers are given tremendous discretion under this particular piece of legislation, Bill C-49. It is up to the police officer to decide whether or not to charge a particular person, for whatever reason. He or she has that discretion under this legislation. While we have the utmost respect for police officers and police force in Canada we have to ensure that a discretion of this magnitude is not given to them because it just might be, and it is likely to be, misused. If a particular officer does not like a particular person for whatever reason
then he or she can decide that that person is impeding the free flow of pedestrian traffic or that that person is attempting to stop a motor vehicle. One can see the problems associated with the vagueness of this particular piece of legislation and the reason it will be turfed out of court. Let me come to the most offensive section of this particular piece of legislation, proposed Subsection 1(c) which states, and I quote:
Every person who in a public place or in any place open to public view (c) stops or attempts to stop any person or in any manner comunicates or
attempts to communicate with any person
for the purpose of engaging in prostitution-
What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? If that is not vague, I do not know what is. What does it mean to attempt to communicate? I am sure Hon. Members in the House, and many Canadians, could think of examples of what it means to attempt to communicate. Is winking an attempt to communicate for the purpose of prostitution? How about if you wave? If any one of us is walking down the street one day and a person unbeknown to us waves at us and we wave back, and that person happens to be a prostitute, I would submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that a police officer could charge that person who is the prostitute and anyone of us in the House, if the officer wanted to. That could be the result of this particular piece of legislation.
I say to Hon. Members opposite to beware of liberal police officers because they could charge you. What would the consequences be to Hon. Members opposite of a charge under Section 195.1 of the Criminal Code of Canada? I need not tell them that their political careers would be destroyed as well as their family life. In any case, they would have a lot of explaining to do to their constituents and to their families. This Bill is offensive on a civil libertarian basis because of the vagueness of this particular piece of legislation. It does not define what it means to attempt to communicate with any person.
Bill C-49 in proposed Subsection 195.1(2) defines what a "public place" means. A "public place" according to this Bill includes any place to which the public has access as of right or by invitation-that would include, of course, shopping malls, bars, lobbies of office buildings, any place where the public has the right of access-expressed or implied, and any motor vehicle located in a public place or in any place open to public view. If one has his car parked in his driveway, someone from the street could look to see what is happening in his car, or if the curtains of a home were open, a pedestrian walking by could look into that home to see if there was an attempt to communicate or direct communication for the purpose of prostitution. In that case, a police officer could lay a charge.
Hon. Members opposite may laugh and say: "Police officers would not do that. They are responsible people". However, you and I know, Mr. Speaker, as well as Hon. Members opposite, that we have to ensure that the discretion given to police officers and others who have to enforce the law have to be limited and that our laws, in order to be good laws, must be
November 20, 1985

certain and definite so a Canadian will know when he or she is committing a criminal offence.
1 will conclude by saying I have considerable regret and chagrin that the Conservatives have brought forward this Bill and have decided not to amend it in order to address the civil libertarian concerns which have been expressed by a great number of Canadians. It is regrettable. We hope that the Government will see the wisdom of its folly and bring in that comprehensive piece of legislation but it is obvious that this Government will not. I simply ask the Government to read my submissions in a year or two years' time and perhaps it will see that what I have said here today holds true.

speechtext: What I meant to say, Mr. Speaker, is that the Conservative Government is totally lacking in wisdom by bringing forward this particular piece of legislation. It is displaying an abysmal folly by bringing it forward. That is what 1 meant.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to say a very few words with

November 20, 1985
The Governor General's Act
respect to third reading of this Act. This Act essentially amends different Acts to increase the salaries of judges, Lieutenant Governors of the Provinces and the Governor General.
The Constitution of Canada imposes upon Parliament the duty to fix and provide the salaries, allowances and pensions of the federally appointed judiciary. It is a difficult duty, although no doubt it seemed fairly straightforward to the Fathers of Confederation when they determined upon the text of Section 100 of what was then the British North America Act. Acting pursuant to this provision, Parliament is expected to balance the needs and expectations of the judiciary with its own responsibility to use the money of the taxpayers wisely and to the best effect. It is a duty only Parliament can perform. By virtue of the wording of Section 100, this duty cannot be delegated to any other body. It is a duty that is often embarrassing and distasteful to both Members of Parliament and members of the judiciary since it requires a public debate upon the remuneration of men and women who, as a result, may be subjected to generalized abuse but who, by their offices, are denied the privilege of public reply. It carries with it the danger of politicizing judicial compensation issues and, unless the levels of compensation are reviewed at regular intervals, the danger also of inequity and unfairness to the judiciary if salaries and other benefits are permitted to fall behind on the basis of leading economic indicators.
Judicial salaries have in fact suffered erosion since 1981 when an indexing formula was first provided to cushion the effects of inflation between parliamentary reviews. Indexing has had the effect of permitting Governments and Parliament to defer consideration of the salary issue in the comforting knowledge that the judiciary were receiving some increase each year without the necessity for full public debate and legislative action. This tendency has been further reinforced by the provision for triennial commissions to review the adequacy of judicial salaries and benefits.
Two years have passed since the report of the first commission on judges' salaries and benefits was tabled in Parliament. At its 1985 annual meeting, the Canadian Bar Association passed a resolution deploring the delay in dealing with the Lang Report and calling for its implementation forthwith. While we are aware of the serious delay which has ensued, the Government also accepts that its mandate for Fiscal restraint and the protection of the nation's economic interests will not permit full acceptance of the Lang Commission's recommendations. Accordingly, we have sought to arrive at adequate compensation for the judiciary while recognizing the fact that we continue in a period of economic recovery and fiscal restraint.
Very briefly, what is intended is that the salary of a judge of a provincial superior court which, as of April 1, 1985, was $93,800 will be increased by this Bill to $105,000. With respect to District Court judges, their salaries will be pegged at $5,000 under the salary level from year to year of a superior court judge.
With respect to the Governor General, the annual salary will be raised from $48,666, its current level, to a level of
$70,000. With respect to the Lieutenant Governors of the provinces, the increase will be to $69,000.
We have heard speeches on this matter and the Minister appeared before the committee to testify with respect to his views on these matters. There were no amendments at report stage. I hope for the sake of the judiciary and other people involved that this matter can have the most prompt attention of the House so that we can implement it and make it law.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and make a few brief remarks on this legislation. The position of members of the New Democratic Party in relation to this legislation was stated clearly at the time of the second reading debate and subsequently when the distinguished Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) appeared before the legislative committee which was considering this Bill. I do not now intend to repeat the arguments we made at that time. However, 1 do want to put on the record our opposition to this legislation.
While no one in this House would in any way deny the integral and vital role played by the judiciary in our legal system, certainly it is not our view that we should be increasing the discrepancies between the wealthy and the poor in Canadian society. At a time of restraint when basic social programs which provide essential social services to the poor are being cut back, and when we are attacking the deficit, an increase in the salaries of a group who are in relative terms privileged economically cannot be justified.
We as Parliamentarians have the obligation to allocate scarce resources among competing ends. If there are additional dollars to be spent, I suggest that they should be spent in assisting those at the bottom end of the economic scale and not those who are already very well paid by any standard of comparison. Instead of increasing the gap between the rich and poor we should be reducing it.
The suggestion has been made that it is essential to increase the salaries of judges in order to recruit more qualified and capable personnel. First, I would suggest that the Canadian Bar Association report on the independence of the judiciary made very clear that that suggestion is without foundation. I would like to quote from that report as follows:
-it is neither necessary nor desirable to establish judicial salaries at such a level as to match the judge's earnings before appointment to the bench. The most obvious reason for this is that such a policy would tend to attract people to the bench for purely financial reasons. The sort of person who would accept a position on the bench because it paid well is not the sort of person who would make the best judge.
Rather the sort of person we would wish to see on the bench are those who appreciate the honour of being a judge and who see as part of their reward the satisfaction of serving society on the bench.
I would remind Hon. Members that in calculating the over-all level of judicial compensation, we must remember as well that there is a very, very rich pension scheme for federal judicial appointees. It has been suggested by some, including some members of the judiciary, that the contributions made by members of the federal judiciary to their own pension plan in some way undermines the independence of the judiciary. I
November 20, 1985

suggest that any statement to that effect is without foundation, and should the Supreme Court of Canada rule in the Beauregard case that in fact the legislation which requires the members of the judiciary to contribute to their pension plans is in fact within the powers of Parliament, Parliament should not take any steps to remove the contributions of members of the federal judiciary.
I would note that there are some flaws in the present judicial pension scheme. These flaws have been identified by a number of commissions. Perhaps one of the most glaring flaws is that those who have served more than 10 years but less than 15 years are not entitled to any pension whatsoever. I suggest that we look at some sort of prorated pension for members of the bench who have served Canada with distinction during that particular period of time.
We also have to look at the method of the appointment of judges. The Canadian Bar Association has recommended substantial changes to the manner in which judicial appointments are made. In August of this year it issued a report which constitutes a scathing criticism of the current method of judicial appointment. It finds that the quality of the Canadian judiciary is high. However, it also finds that in some provinces politics play too great a role in the selection of candidates for the bench. It recommends one form of judicial appointment process which I think we should certainly look at.
What we must recognize is that the present system, which allows for political patronage to far too great an extent, is one
The Governor General's Act
which has no place in a democratic society, particularly at a time when the role of the judiciary is being enhanced by the adoption of an entrenched Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
At third reading stage 1 wanted to put on the record these brief points with respect to some of our concerns about this legislation. I wish to note that, federally, the New Democratic Party opposes this Bill and will continue to call for legislation and policy which will reduce the gap between rich and poor in Canada instead of increasing the gap, as this Bill would do.
